newsitem.title: IRAQ: Oil deal delay harms Iraqis' health - minister.
newsitem.headline: Oil deal delay harms Iraqis' health - minister.

text.p: Iraq's health minister said on Monday the health situation in his country was serious and condemned U.S. attempts to delay the implementation of Iraq's oil-for-food deal with the United Nations.

"We are suffering from a really grave situation," Umeed Madhat Mubarak told reporters. Asked about Washington's insistance to suspend the oil-for-food scheme Iraq signed with the United Nations on May 20, he said: "From a humanitarian point of view we should condemn that."
U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali delayed implementing the deal after Iraqi forces attacked Kurdish rebels in northern Iraq on August 31, saying he feared for the safety of U.N. staff.
U.S. President Bill Clinton also said he wanted the plan suspended for the time being.
"It is inhuman and unfair," Mubarak, a cardiologist, said. "It is a unilateral decision made by the U.S. administration."

Mubarak said Iraq had been preparing to receive medical supplies under the deal which would have enabled it to resume emergency activities in hospitals, improve the situation in the field of preventive medicine and provide people suffering from chronic diseases with "proper dosages of drugs".
He said 168 new-born babies were now dying out of 1,000 live births, up from 24 before the United Nations imposed a strict trade embargo on Iraq in 1990 for invading Kuwait.
Mubarak said more than one million Iraqi children were malnourished because government rations were hardly enough to provide one third of their food needs.
Certain communicable diseases, such as malaria, cholera, diphtheria and typhoid, which Iraq had obliterated prior to the embargo, were now a serious problem for his ministry, he said.

The trade sanctions bar Iraq from exporting oil to world markets. But under the deal with the United Nations, it was to buy food, medicine and other humanitarian supplies worth about $1.13 billion from $2 billion of oil exports over six months.
Mubarak said his ministry was to receive $210 million of that sum.
Asked whether health allocations under the oil-for-food programme would have helped ease Iraqis' suffering, he said: "Definitely yes."
Mubarak said the breakdown of sewage systems, lack of clean water and frequent cuts in power supply further aggravated the health situation in Iraq.

He lambasted Washington for its tough stand on sanctions, saying Iraq had honoured Gulf War obligations which would allow oil exports. "But there is somebody creating problems for dirty political ends and that is the United States," he said.
The minister said the situation in northern Iraq in the aftermath of Iraq's military incursion did not justify putting off the oil-for-food formula.
Mubarak, himself a Kurd from the northern Kurdish city of Sulaimaniya, also criticised Washington over reports of a CIA plot to overthrow the government of President Saddam Hussein.
"The enemies of humanity in Iraq -- on top of them of course the Clinton administration -- can create a problem any day, any hour," he said.
According to a report in the Los Angeles Times, CIA director John Deutch had personally promised to topple Saddam's government before the Iraqi leader sent troops into Kurdish areas.
